overview: This section explains the two kinds of IPv4 addressing you meet in AWS: public IPs, which are unique across the whole internet and let a machine be reached from the WWW, and private IPs, which are unique only inside one network and can be freely reused by other companies. It then introduces the Elastic IP, the only way in this section to give an instance a fixed public IPv4 address, together with its one-instance attachment rule, its 5-per-account limit and the architectural advice to avoid it in favour of DNS names or a Load Balancer. Exam questions use this as a design decision: does the workload need a stable, known public endpoint, and if so, what is the least brittle way to provide it?

coreConcepts.definition: The dotted-decimal address format [0-255].[0-255].[0-255].[0-255] (e.g. 1.160.10.240); the most common format online, allowing 3.7 billion different addresses in the public space, and the only format used in this course.
A newer, longer hexadecimal address format (e.g. 3ffe:1900:4545:3:200:f8ff:fe21:67cf) that solves problems for the Internet of Things (IoT).
An address that identifies a machine on the internet (WWW); it must be unique across the whole web and can be geo-located easily.

An address that identifies a machine only on a private network; it must be unique across that private network, but two different private networks (two companies) can have the same IPs, and only a specified range of IPs can be used as private IPs.
The proxy mechanism by which machines with private IPs connect to the WWW.
A public IPv4 IP that you own for as long as you don't delete it, used when an instance needs a fixed public IP; it can be attached to one instance at a time.
By default an EC2 machine comes with a private IP for the internal AWS Network and a public IP for the WWW.
When you stop and then start an EC2 instance, it can change its public IP.
The public-facing gateway address (e.g. 149.140.72.10, 253.144.139.205 in the section's example diagram) through which a private network reaches the WWW.
Rapidly reassigning the Elastic IP to another instance in your account, which masks the failure of an instance or software.
The recommended alternative to an Elastic IP: use a random public IP and register a DNS name to it.
The other recommended alternative: front the instances with a Load Balancer and don't use a public IP on the instance.
Remote access to an EC2 machine; you cannot use the private IP because you are not in the same network, so you can only use the public IP.

mustRemember: Public IP must be unique across the whole web — no two machines can share the same public IP.
Private IP must be unique across the private network, but two different private networks (two companies) can have the same IPs.
Public IPs can be geo-located easily.
Machines with private IPs connect to the WWW using a NAT + internet gateway (a proxy).
Only a specified range of IPs can be used as private IP.
Stopping and then starting an EC2 instance can change its public IP.
An Elastic IP can be attached to one instance at a time.
You can only have 5 Elastic IPs in your account (you can ask AWS to increase that).
Elastic IPs often reflect poor architectural decisions — prefer a random public IP with a registered DNS name, or a Load Balancer with no public IP.
By default an EC2 machine comes with a private IP (internal AWS network) and a public IP (for the WWW).
To SSH into an EC2 instance you can only use the public IP, not the private IP, because you are not in the same network.
IPv4 format is [0-255].[0-255].[0-255].[0-255], allowing 3.7 billion different addresses in the public space.

keyComparisons.difference: A public IP is reachable and unique on the whole internet and is geo-locatable, while a private IP is only unique and reachable inside its own private network.

keyComparisons.items: Elastic IP vs default EC2 public IP
keyComparisons.difference: The default public IP can change when the instance is stopped and started; an Elastic IP stays fixed (you own it until you delete it).

keyComparisons.items: Elastic IP vs DNS name on a random public IP
keyComparisons.difference: A DNS name keeps a stable, user-facing endpoint without consuming a scarce Elastic IP, and hides the underlying changing public IP.
An Elastic IP hard-wires one address to one instance; a Load Balancer fronts multiple instances and lets you not use a public IP on the instances at all.
IPv4 is the common 4-octet dotted address (3.7 billion public addresses); IPv6 is newer, longer hexadecimal and solves problems for IoT.

keyComparisons.items: SSH via public IP vs SSH via private IP
keyComparisons.difference: From outside AWS you can only SSH using the public IP; the private IP is unusable because you are not in the same network.

commonMisunderstandings: Two companies cannot have the same private IP range — in fact they can; private IPs only have to be unique within their own private network.
You should SSH to an instance using its private IP — you can only use the public IP, because you are not in the same network.
An EC2 instance's default public IP is permanent — it can change when the instance is stopped and started, which is exactly why Elastic IPs exist.
One Elastic IP can be shared across several instances at once — it can be attached to only one instance at a time.
Elastic IPs are the recommended way to give a web tier a stable endpoint — they often reflect poor architectural decisions; prefer a DNS name on a random public IP, or a Load Balancer.
A private IP lets a machine be identified on the internet — it only identifies the machine on its private network; WWW access goes through NAT + internet gateway.
mentalModels: Think of a public IP as a street address that must be unique worldwide, and a private IP as a room number that only has to be unique inside its own building — every building can have a room 101.
Think of NAT + internet gateway as a receptionist/proxy: private machines talk to the outside world through it, without exposing their own private numbers.
Think of an Elastic IP as a reserved parking space that is yours until you give it back — and you can only park one car in it at a time.
Think of the stop/start public IP change as a dynamic lease, and a DNS name or Load Balancer as the sign outside the building that stays valid even when the tenant changes.
Think of Elastic IPs as a scarce, blunt tool (5 per account) that you reach for only when nothing better fits.
edgeCases: If you need more than 5 Elastic IPs, you can ask AWS to increase the limit.
One Elastic IP can be rapidly remapped to another instance in your account to mask the failure of an instance or software.
An Elastic IP is a public IPv4 address you own as long as you don't delete it.
A Load Balancer approach avoids using a public IP on the instance at all.
The private IP range is restricted: only a specified range of IPs can be used as private IP.

whenToUse.situation: An instance must keep the same public IPv4 address through stop/start cycles
You want a stable, human-facing endpoint without consuming a scarce Elastic IP
whenToUse.use: Register a DNS name to a random public IP

whenToUse.situation: Multiple instances behind a single stable entry point, with no public IP on the instances
whenToUse.use: Load Balancer (don't use a public IP)

whenToUse.situation: You need to fail over from a failed instance or software quickly
whenToUse.use: Rapidly remap the Elastic IP to another instance in your account

whenToUse.situation: You need to SSH into an EC2 instance from your own machine
whenToUse.use: Connect to the instance's public IP

whenToUse.situation: A machine on a private network must reach the WWW

patternsToRecognize.signal: Question says the instance must keep the same public IP after stop/start
Scenario mentions a limited number of Elastic IPs or asks for the AWS-friendly design
patternsToRecognize.indicates: DNS name or Load Balancer instead of Elastic IP
Private IP ranges only need to be unique within a network

patternsToRecognize.signal: Question asks why the instance cannot be reached by its private IP from the internet
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Private IP is internal-only; you need the public IP or NAT + internet gateway

patternsToRecognize.signal: Requirement to hide an instance failure by moving the address
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Remap the Elastic IP to another instance

patternsToRecognize.signal: Design asks for a stable endpoint for a scalable web tier
patternsToRecognize.indicates: Load Balancer rather than a public IP per instance

examTraps.trap: Assuming an Elastic IP can front a fleet of instances simultaneously
examTraps.correction: An Elastic IP attaches to one instance at a time; use a Load Balancer for a fleet.

examTraps.trap: Assuming you can have unlimited Elastic IPs
examTraps.correction: The limit is 5 per account; you can ask AWS to increase it.

examTraps.trap: Choosing an Elastic IP as the 'best-practice' answer for every stable-endpoint question
examTraps.correction: The section says to try to avoid Elastic IPs; preferred answers are a DNS name on a random public IP or a Load Balancer with no public IP.

examTraps.trap: Believing a public IP must be unique inside a VPC rather than on the internet
examTraps.correction: A public IP must be unique across the whole web; it is the private IP that only needs uniqueness within the private network.

examTraps.trap: Thinking the EC2 public IP is fixed after creation
examTraps.correction: Stop and start can change the public IP; only an Elastic IP stays fixed.

examTraps.trap: Using the private IP for SSH from outside AWS
examTraps.correction: You can only SSH using the public IP because you are not in the same network.

beyondSource: Elastic IPs are allocated per Region and, by design, cannot be attached across Regions; out of scope here, but a common distractor framing.

Modern AWS accounts may start with a different default Elastic IP quota than 5 (quotas were later tightened for new accounts); the source's 5-per-account figure is the value a question is most likely to test unless stated otherwise.
